title: Unmasking the Thermo‐Pollution Nexus: A Multimodal Decomposition of LST‐AOD Dynamics in a Tropical Megacity
content:
Abstract

Rapid urbanization in tropical sub-Saharan Africa intensifies the thermo-pollution nexus, the interplay between land surface temperature (LST) and aerosol pollution (AOD), with implications for environmental health and sustainability. This study examines the spatiotemporal dynamics and statistical interactions between AOD and LST in the Lagos Metropolitan Area (January 2017–August 2025). Using a multimodal decomposition framework integrating principal component analysis (PCA), seasonal-trend decomposition using Loess (STL), and lagged correlation analysis implemented in Google Earth Engine and Python, the study quantifies variability, trends, and lead-lag structure. Results show no significant long-term monotonic trends in either AOD or LST, indicating the dominance of strong seasonal cycles. AOD peaks during the Harmattan dry season (November–March; >1.25), whereas LST maxima (30.5°C) occur about 1 month later. Contemporaneous monthly AOD–LST correlation is weak, but positive associations emerge when AOD leads LST by 1–3 months (strongest at 2 months), consistent with a recurring seasonal phase offset. A Harmattan-excluded sensitivity test (April–October) weakens the coupling, leaving only a modest significant 1-month lead, suggesting that seasonal regime differences and covarying meteorology shape the lag structure. PCA identifies two dominant modes: a synchronous seasonal component (52% variance) and a contrasting/differential component (48%). Extreme-event analysis shows that high-AOD episodes are strongly seasonal, whereas heat waves are episodic and rarely co-occur, highlighting event-scale decoupling. Overall, seasonal forcing and meteorology govern AOD–LST relationships in Lagos, informing urban climate resilience and public health planning.
